reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A chronic granulomatous infection caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi that most often involves the nose and nasopharynx
Presents with a friable, reddish, highly vascular polypoidal mass that bleeds easily and is classically studded with white dots representing sporangia, giving a strawberry-like appearance
Common symptoms are unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and a mass that may be visible or prolapse into the nasopharynx
It is endemic in parts of the Indian subcontinent and is linked to exposure to stagnant water and bathing in ponds
Diagnosis is confirmed histologically by the characteristic sporangia containing endospores in a granulomatous stroma
Treatment is complete surgical excision of the lesion, and cauterising the base helps reduce recurrence and bleeding
Recurrence is well recognised because of local spread of endospores, so meticulous removal and base cautery are important
The lesion bleeds readily, so care during examination and excision is needed to control haemorrhage
reference.pathophysiology: Rhinosporidiosis is caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi, now regarded as an aquatic protistan parasite, which is thought to enter the mucosa through minor trauma after contact with contaminated stagnant water. The organism proliferates within the mucosa, maturing through trophic stages into large sporangia packed with endospores. Rupture of a sporangium releases endospores that seed adjacent tissue, driving formation of highly vascular polypoidal granulomatous masses. The rich vascularity accounts for the marked tendency to bleed, and local dissemination of endospores explains frequent recurrence after incomplete removal.
additionalDifferentials: Other granulomatous nasal infections such as tuberculosis
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy to define the vascular polypoidal mass and its extent
Histopathology of the excised tissue to demonstrate sporangia and endospores
Assessment of haemoglobin where recurrent epistaxis has occurred
Imaging in extensive disease to define spread beyond the nasal cavity
redFlags: Brisk or recurrent epistaxis from the friable vascular mass requiring measures to secure haemostasis
Disseminated disease involving sites beyond the nose such as the eye, larynx, or skin
Airway compromise from a large nasopharyngeal mass
Rapid change or atypical features raising concern for coexisting malignancy
reference.prognosis: Complete excision with cautery of the base usually gives a good outcome, but recurrence is common owing to local spread of endospores, and disease occasionally disseminates to other mucosal sites; the condition is chronic and can be troublesome to eradicate fully.
pitfalls: Underestimating the vascularity and provoking significant bleeding during biopsy or removal
Incomplete excision that leaves endospores and leads to recurrence
Mistaking the mass for a simple polyp and not obtaining histology
Overlooking disease at other sites in disseminated cases
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Complete surgical excision of the polypoidal mass, which is the mainstay of treatment
Cauterisation or electrocoagulation of the lesion base to reduce recurrence and control bleeding
Adjuvant dapsone to suppress residual disease and lower the recurrence rate
Control of intraoperative and recurrent epistaxis, with transfusion and correction of anaemia where bleeding has been heavy
Histological confirmation of the excised tissue to demonstrate sporangia and endospores
Advise avoidance of bathing in stagnant pond water to reduce reinfection
Endoscopic surveillance for recurrence given local spread of endospores
